title: Scalable near-real-time Bayesian phylogenetics for outbreaks with Delphy.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the whole public data repository (870 files, 826 MB) via the GitHub API, then downloaded and parsed 11 files with no login: the H5N1 (bird flu) alignment (exactly 1,889 sequences, all 13,136 bases), the Ebola alignment (81 sequences, 18,959 bases), four metadata CSVs (H5N1 2,850 rows; SARS-CoV-2 773 rows; mpox 177 rows; Ebola 81 rows), one simulation ground-truth tree (100 tips, Newick format), one simulation parameter file, and one Delphy MCMC trace log (5,004 posterior samples, columns TreeHeight/clockRate/kappa/ePopSize/growthRate). I joined the H5N1 alignment headers to the metadata myself: all 1,889 strain names matched after splitting the header on '|', and 1,888 carry a US state label across 15 states (California 808, Colorado 271, Texas 240 ... Utah 3), sampled 2024-03-10 to 2024-12-26, every one from cattle.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Sequence counts per outbreak as reported in the bioRxiv preprint (SARS-CoV-2 757, Zika 174, mpox 177, Ebola 81, H5N1 1,889), the claimed 2-3 orders-of-magnitude speed-up over BEAST, and the 100,000-sequence scalability result. I did not read the Nature version (paywalled, no PubMed Central copy) and did not open the Zika or 100,000-tip simulation files.

a1_downloadable.note: Public GitHub repository, no login: I downloaded 11 files successfully. Caveat seen in the README: the largest run-result files (.dphy, 24-302 MB) were too big for GitHub and are 'available upon request' by email, and the data repository carries no licence file.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The repository is an archive of software benchmark runs, not a modelling table: alignments, BEAST configuration files, MCMC trace logs, thousands of sampled trees and PDF figures. For the paper's actual subject (phylogenetic inference) the target - tree topology, node dates, clade support - exists only inside NEXUS/Newick tree files and must be constructed by parsing trees and matching clades between an inferred tree and a reference tree. The only ready-made label columns are geographic ones in the metadata CSVs, which belong to a different and much weaker task.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are real sequence data, not accessions: I counted 1,889 aligned H5N1 genomes (13,136 bases each) and 81 aligned Ebola genomes (18,959 bases each) directly in the FASTA files.

a4_units_stated.note: Not really applicable - the only categorical labels (US state, region) need no units. The numeric MCMC trace columns (TreeHeight, clockRate) have conventional but nowhere-stated units (years; substitutions per site per year), which would be a silent-error risk if used.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL at the correct unit of analysis. For the paper's task the example is a whole dataset, and there are 13: 5 real outbreaks plus 8 simulations (constant and exponential population growth at 100/1,000/10,000/100,000 tips, one random seed each, identical substitution parameters). The sub-task that does have rows - predicting US state from an H5N1 genome - has 1,888 labelled sequences but they are all cattle from one 2024 outbreak.

a6_fits_laptop.note: The whole repository is 826 MB; the largest single file I would need (the H5N1 alignment) is 25 MB and loaded instantly. No laptop problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Mostly reconcilable but untidy: the H5N1 alignment has exactly 1,889 sequences as the paper says, yet its metadata CSV has 2,850 rows of which 962 have the state recorded as '-'; the SARS-CoV-2 metadata has 773 rows against 757 sequences claimed, with 258 of 773 clade values blank. The metadata files are supersets, so you can tell which is right.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL for the abundant targets. The posterior clade probabilities, node heights and clock rates in the .trees and .log files are outputs of the MCMC sampler itself, so a model trained on them would be distilling BEAST/Delphy rather than learning anything measured. The simulation ground-truth trees are honest labels but come from the authors' own simulator (sapling) with one fixed parameter set, so anyone wanting them would generate their own rather than use these eight.

existing_models.name: Delphy (this paper's own method; Bayesian phylogenetics via explicit mutation-annotated trees, not machine learning)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reproduces BEAST/BEAST2 posterior estimates on five real outbreak datasets (Ebola 81, Zika 174, mpox 177, SARS-CoV-2 757, H5N1 1,889 sequences) and on eight simulations with known true trees, at up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower runtime; no held-out split in the machine-learning sense.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Scaling and usability for frontline outbreak response; the README also states the authors will not maintain the analysis scripts.

existing_models.name: Phyloformer, a transformer neural network that predicts evolutionary distances between sequences and hence the tree
existing_models.score_and_split: Published in Molecular Biology and Evolution 42(4), 2025; reported as matching maximum-likelihood accuracy under the standard LG+GC evolutionary model and beating it under more complex models, roughly 100x faster; evaluated on simulated alignments and empirical benchmarks.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation beyond the evolutionary models used to generate training simulations.

existing_models.name: PhyloDeep (Voznica et al., 'Deep learning from phylogenies to uncover the epidemiological dynamics of outbreaks')
existing_models.score_and_split: Nature Communications 2022; reported as matching or beating likelihood-based phylodynamic inference while being over 1,000x faster after training; evaluated on simulated trees plus an HIV case study.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Model misspecification - behaviour when the real epidemic does not match the simulation model used for training.

existing_models.name: Neural posterior estimation for epidemiological and phylodynamic models (simulation-based inference)
existing_models.score_and_split: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2026 (preprint bioRxiv 2025.11.25.690436); learns the full posterior directly from simulations, amortised so new datasets are near-instant; evaluated against likelihood-based posteriors on simulations.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Calibration and model criticism when the simulator is wrong.

existing_models.name: Amortized phylodynamic inference with neural Bayes estimators and recursive neural networks (arXiv 2603.08345)
existing_models.score_and_split: 2026 preprint; quantile regression over tree space using a recursive neural network tree encoder, estimating reproduction number, prevalence and cumulative infections through time; evaluated on simulations.

existing_models.name: Deep learning for viral phylogeography (Systematic Biology 73(1), 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports that deep learning and likelihood approaches converge on the same answers for viral phylogeography whether the inference model is right or wrong; evaluated on simulated and real viral datasets.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: That agreement between methods does not imply correctness when the model is misspecified.

backbone.name: None that fits. Nucleotide Transformer / DNABERT-2 / HyenaDNA are genomic-sequence backbones, but the thing to predict here is a tree relating sequences, not a per-sequence property, so a frozen-embedding-plus-head setup does not map onto the task.
backbone.hardware: CPU would suffice for the data volume; the mismatch is conceptual, not computational.
backbone.licence: Delphy code is MIT since December 2025; the separate paper-data repository has no licence file at all, which is a real obstacle to redistributing a derived dataset.

integration.partner_dataset: GISAID / NCBI Influenza Virus Database and the Nextstrain avian-flu build, joinable to the H5N1 sequences; GenBank accessions for the Ebola and mpox sets.
integration.join_key: Influenza strain name (e.g. A/cattle/Texas/24-009108-005/2024) plus SRA run accession, both present in the FASTA headers; GenBank accessions for mpox (e.g. MK783027).
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: A join would only enlarge the same one-outbreak sequence collection; it would not create a question neither source could answer alone.

controls.positive_control: For the simulations only: the true tree from the sapling simulator, so any inference method can be scored against it. For the real outbreaks there is no ground truth, only agreement with BEAST.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable in principle for the geographic sub-task, but the real leakage control needed (grouping by herd or farm) is impossible because no herd identifier is in the metadata.
controls.external_validation: A date column exists for every H5N1 sequence (2024-03-10 to 2024-12-26), so a temporal split is cheap; but it would still be one outbreak, one host and one pathogen.

honest_claim_h3: The most a model built on these files could honestly claim is: 'among 1,888 H5N1 genomes collected from US dairy cattle during the 2024 outbreak, sequence alone predicts the US state of sampling at X% accuracy' - a statement about one outbreak's sampling pattern, heavily confounded by the fact that near-identical sequences come from the same herd, and already answered by published Bayesian phylogeographic analyses.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a viral genome alignment to predict the evolutionary tree and dates that slow Bayesian software would eventually output.
plain_idea.train_on: Aligned viral genomes with their collection dates. In this repository that means 13 datasets in total: 5 real outbreaks (81 to 1,889 genomes each) and 8 computer simulations, which is 13 training examples at the level that matters.
plain_idea.predict: The dated evolutionary tree, or summaries of it such as when a lineage first appeared. The true answer comes either from the simulator (known by construction) or from a long BEAST run, which is itself a computational estimate rather than a measurement.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Outbreak responders need tree estimates in minutes, not days, and a learned shortcut would deliver that. But Delphy itself already delivers the speed-up without machine learning, and five other groups have published learned shortcuts since 2022.

more_or_better_data.why: Phyloformer and PhyloDeep train on hundreds of thousands of simulated alignments generated on demand; this repository contains 8 simulations with one random seed each and identical substitution parameters, plus 5 real outbreaks totalling roughly 3,100 sequences.

confidence_score.why: Each dataset has only two independent Delphy chains (runs 'a' and 'b'), so replicate spread is available for a handful of datasets, and the existing neural posterior estimation methods already output full calibrated posteriors by design.

models_beatable.why: Phyloformer (Molecular Biology and Evolution, 2025), neural posterior estimation (Proceedings B, 2026) and neural Bayes estimators (2026) are recent, open or semi-open, transformer and recursive-neural-network based, and already evaluated against likelihood-based posteriors on simulations where truth is known.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on the first condition: there is no feature/label table to run a baseline on, and the 13 datasets here are far too few to train anything, so adding them to an existing model's training set would change nothing measurable.

ml_idea: The project considered was a learned fast surrogate for Bayesian phylogenetics: feed an alignment plus sampling dates to a neural network and have it emit the dated tree or its posterior summaries, using Delphy and BEAST as the reference. It dies on two checklist killers at once. There is no feature/label table in the repository - every target must be reconstructed by parsing NEXUS and Newick tree files and matching clades between trees (A2) - and the abundant targets are themselves MCMC outputs, so training on them distils BEAST rather than learning biology (A8). The honest unit of analysis is the dataset, and there are 13 of them. The one genuine label column, US state for 1,888 H5N1 cattle genomes, supports only a single-outbreak phylogeography task with no herd identifier to split on, which a nearest-neighbour sequence lookup would largely solve.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond the downloads I ran: the files are small (826 MB total repository, 25 MB largest alignment) so compute is never the constraint. The 40 hours is the tree-parsing and clade-matching work needed to turn thousands of sampled NEXUS trees into any kind of table, which is exactly the cost that makes it not worth doing.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the independent training examples at the right unit. I did it: 13 datasets (5 real outbreaks, 8 simulations), and 1,888 sequences in the single largest labelled set, all cattle from one 2024 outbreak.

verdict_reason: Fails A2 and A8. The public data repository is an archive of software benchmark runs - alignments, BEAST configuration files, MCMC trace logs, thousands of sampled trees, PDFs - with no feature/label table anywhere; any phylogenetic target has to be constructed by parsing and matching tree files. The targets that are abundant (clade posterior support, node heights, clock rates) are outputs of the MCMC sampler itself, so a model trained on them distils BEAST rather than learning from measurement. At the honest unit of analysis there are 13 datasets. The one real label column - US state for 1,888 H5N1 cattle genomes, which I verified joins cleanly - supports only a single-outbreak, single-host phylogeography task with no herd identifier available to split on, in a field already served by six open or semi-open learned methods (Phyloformer, PhyloDeep, neural posterior estimation, neural Bayes estimators and others).
